say: Assalam o alaikum. I'm Hassan Ali Mehdi, and this is BoltaNote, which means 'the talking note'. You point your phone at a Pakistani banknote, and it tells you the value out loud, in Urdu.

Pakistan has about one point one million blind people, and most daily payments are still made in cash. Our seven notes differ only a little in size, so a blind person usually has to ask a stranger which note is which, and trust the answer. Mixing up a five hundred and a five thousand costs four and a half thousand rupees.

BoltaNote is just a web page. It reads the camera four times a second and speaks the value in Urdu or English, with a recorded voice, so it works even on phones that have no Urdu speech. It stays silent when it's unsure, because saying a wrong amount is worse than saying nothing. Once loaded, it works offline, and it also vibrates a code and works with screen readers.

I trained on a public dataset of three thousand six hundred real phone photos: seven notes, front and back, many folded or half visible. I added a 'no note' class with a thousand everyday photos, so the model learns when to stay quiet.

Before trusting any number, I checked whether the test photos were really new. I hashed every photo, and found that 339 of the 402 test photos in a second public currency dataset are near-copies of the first. Only 63 were genuinely new. Without this check, my external test would have looked perfect and meant nothing.

Training images are changed on the GPU every time they're seen: any angle, too close, half out of frame, fingers over the note, dim or yellow light, and blur. No mirror flips, because the camera never sees a mirrored note.

I compared a CNN trained from scratch with two phone networks pretrained on ImageNet: MobileNet version three and the new MobileNet version four. On photos from the same dataset, all three are almost perfect. On photos taken by other people, the difference shows: transfer learning holds up far better. I deployed MobileNetV3-Large, the best on validation, and also the fastest.

Here are the honest numbers. 100% on unseen photos from the same dataset, but 92% on photos by other people, and on those photos it never said a wrong amount. The first number mostly shows how alike the dataset's photos are; the others are what a real user would get.

The most important design decision is when to speak. On ordinary validation photos the model is almost never wrong, so any threshold looks safe. So I calibrated on a stress test: every validation photo four times, with the hard augmentations. The app speaks only above 0.68 confidence, and only when three frames in a row agree.
Here's the live demo. I open the site on my phone, tap Start camera, and hold a note in front of it. It reads several frames a second and speaks the value, with nothing installed.

Its limits: the training photos show only a few physical notes per value, it knows the current note designs but not the State Bank's new series, it reads one note at a time, and it doesn't detect counterfeits. Next: worn notes, counting a whole handful, and a test with blind users.
Everything is open: the website, the code, the weights and the data splits are all linked. Thank you, Dr. Munir Ahmad, and thank you for watching.
